moduleTitle: SQE1 · Wills and Administration of Estates
title: Personal representatives' powers, protections, and personal liability
subtitle: Appropriation, advancement, devastavit, and the defences that actually matter
objectives: Explain the modernised powers of appropriation and advancement under the Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014
State what devastavit means and why a personal representative's liability for it is personal, not just professional
Apply the s 27 Trustee Act 1925 advertisement procedure and the Benjamin order to a fact pattern to identify whether a personal representative is protected

leadingAuthorities.citation: Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014, ss 41-42
leadingAuthorities.role: Modernises the personal representative's powers of appropriation and advancement
General powers of management given to personal representatives during administration
Statutory protection by advertisement against unknown claims
Court order permitting distribution on an assumed basis where a beneficiary's existence or whereabouts is uncertain

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students learn the powers of appropriation and advancement as a checklist and forget they exist to solve a single practical problem: a personal representative who gets it wrong can be made to pay out of their own pocket. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You can name the powers — this lesson is about when a solicitor actually needs to reach for them.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the definitions here. The test pool is weighted towards scenario questions: expect a fact pattern and a 'what should the solicitor advise' stem, not a request to define a term.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down on Parts 1 and 2 — devastavit and the basic appropriation power are the foundation everything else in this lesson sits on.

overview.hook: A personal representative isn't an employee of the estate, protected by a corporate structure if something goes wrong. They are personally on the hook — their own house, their own savings — for a mistake in administering someone else's affairs. Almost nobody who agrees to act as an executor for a friend or relative realises this. This lesson is about the exposure, and about the handful of tools the law gives a careful PR to close it down.

parts.heading: Devastavit: why 'I did my best' is not a defence
parts.voice: direct — names the risk before softening it with the tools that manage it
body: A personal representative (PR) who wastes, misapplies, or loses estate assets through a breach of their duties commits what the old cases call a devastavit — literally, 'he has wasted'. The consequence is not a fine or a professional sanction. It is personal liability: the PR must make good the loss to the estate out of their own assets.

This surprises students because most other actors in a legal problem are protected by something — a company's limited liability, an insurer, a corporate veil. A PR administering an estate has none of that by default. Pay the wrong creditor first and there isn't enough left for the right one; distribute to a beneficiary who turns out not to exist; sell an asset carelessly below value — each is capable of founding a devastavit claim by a beneficiary or an unpaid creditor.

The standard the PR is held to is that of the ordinary prudent person of business managing their own affairs — higher, under s 1 Trustee Act 2000, where the PR is acting in a professional capacity for reward. The rest of this lesson is about the statutory and case-law tools that let a careful PR administer the estate without carrying that exposure indefinitely.

components.definition: A breach of duty by a personal representative in administering an estate — misapplying, wasting, or losing estate assets — that exposes the PR to personal liability to make good the loss.

interaction.prompt: If a personal representative commits a devastavit, whose assets are used to make good the loss to the estate?
options: The personal representative's own personal assets
The estate's assets alone — the PR is never personally liable
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. That personal exposure is exactly why the protective devices later in this lesson matter so much in practice.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again — the whole point of devastavit is that liability lands on the PR personally, not merely on the estate they are administering.

parts.heading: The modernised power of appropriation
parts.voice: practical — walks through what the power lets a PR do and what changed in 2014
body: A PR does not have to sell every estate asset and distribute cash. The power of appropriation lets a PR transfer a specific asset — a house, shares, a car — to a beneficiary in satisfaction (in whole or part) of that beneficiary's entitlement, valuing the asset as at the date of appropriation, and without needing to sell it first.

Before the Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014, exercising this power in favour of a beneficiary who was a minor or otherwise lacked capacity required a separate formal consent from a trustee other than the PR, even where the PR was themselves the trustee of that beneficiary's share — an artificial extra step that duplicated a decision the same people had already made. The 2014 Act removed that duplicated consent requirement where the PR is also the relevant trustee, while preserving the underlying safeguard: no appropriation may prejudice a specific beneficiary, and the consent of a beneficiary who is of full age and capacity is still required where their interest is affected.

The power matters most where an estate has an asset a beneficiary actually wants to keep — a family home, a shareholding in a private company — rather than forcing a sale purely to divide cash evenly.

components.label: Appropriation in practice
points: The PR transfers a specific asset in satisfaction of a beneficiary's entitlement, rather than selling it
The asset is valued at the date of appropriation, not the date of death
No appropriation may be made to the prejudice of any specific legatee
Consent of an adult, capacitous beneficiary whose interest is affected is still required
The 2014 Act removed the need for a separate trustee consent where the PR and the trustee are the same person

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that means the PRs in this scenario can appropriate the house without a separate trustee consent.
interaction.scenarioText: An estate includes a house worth £300,000. The residuary beneficiary, Priya, is an adult with full capacity and wants to take the house rather than have it sold. The two PRs administering the estate are also the trustees of Priya's share.
tappableSpans: Priya, is an adult with full capacity
wants to take the house rather than have it sold
the two PRs administering the estate are also the trustees
interaction.correctSpan: the two PRs administering the estate are also the trustees
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct — it is the PRs and trustees being the same people that removes the old duplicated consent requirement under the 2014 Act reforms. Priya's own consent as an adult beneficiary is still needed, but that is a separate point.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The relevant fact is about who holds which role, not about the asset or the beneficiary's wishes. Look for the fact that tells you the PRs and the trustees are the same people.

parts.heading: The modernised power of advancement
parts.voice: scenario-led — shows why the pre-2014 limit was a practical problem
body: Where a beneficiary has a future or contingent interest — a trust for a child at 25, say — the person holding the property on trust may want to release money to that beneficiary before their interest vests, to pay for education, a deposit, or a medical need. That is the power of advancement.

Before the 2014 reforms, this power was capped: only half of a beneficiary's presumptive share could ever be advanced in this way, however clear the need and however comfortably the rest of the trust fund could bear it. The 2014 Act removed that cap for trusts within its scope, allowing the whole of a beneficiary's presumptive share to be advanced, subject to the trustees' ordinary duty to exercise the power reasonably and with regard to the interests of anyone else who might be prejudiced.
The change matters in practice wherever a family trust needs to respond flexibly to one beneficiary's genuine need without artificially starving that advance at the fifty per cent mark.

components.definition: The power to pay or apply trust capital for the benefit of a beneficiary with a future or contingent interest, before that interest vests; since the 2014 reforms, up to the whole of the beneficiary's presumptive share may be advanced.

interaction.prompt: A trust holds £200,000 for Tomas, contingent on reaching 25. He is now 20 and needs £150,000 for a course of medical treatment. The trustees consider this a reasonable use of the power and no one else's interest is prejudiced. Can they advance the £150,000?
options: No — advancement is still capped at half the presumptive share, so at most £100,000 can be advanced
Yes — since the 2014 reforms, the whole of a beneficiary's presumptive share can be advanced, not just half
No — advancement can never be exercised before the beneficiary's interest vests
interaction.explanation: The old 50% ceiling was removed by the Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014. The only remaining constraints are the trustees' duty to exercise the power reasonably and the need to have regard to anyone else with an interest that might be prejudiced — neither of which is in issue on these facts.

parts.heading: Section 27 protection: advertising for claims
parts.voice: procedural — treats this as a checklist a solicitor would actually follow
body: A PR cannot realistically wait forever to distribute an estate on the chance that an unknown creditor or beneficiary might one day surface. Section 27 Trustee Act 1925 gives PRs a statutory procedure to close that risk down before distributing.

The PR places a notice in the London Gazette, a newspaper circulating in the area where any land in the estate is situated, and any other notice a court would direct in the circumstances (for example, in a location connected to the deceased's business). The notice invites anyone with a claim against the estate to send details within a stated period of not less than two months.

Once that period expires, the PR may distribute the estate having regard only to the claims of which they then have notice, without personal liability to a claimant who comes forward later. Crucially, that protection runs only in the PR's favour: a claimant who missed the deadline can still pursue the beneficiaries who received the assets, typically by tracing, even though the PR themselves is safe.

components.text: Trustees or personal representatives... may give notice by advertisement in the London Gazette, and in a newspaper circulating in the district in which the land is situated... of their intention to distribute the assets... and requiring any person interested to send in particulars of their claim... within the time... not being less than two months...
elements: Notice in a newspaper circulating where any estate land is situated
Any other notice the circumstances require (e.g. a court direction)
A stated claims period of not less than two months
Distribution only after that period, having regard only to notified claims

interaction.prompt: Put these steps of the s 27 procedure in the correct order.
items: The PR places notices in the London Gazette and a relevant local newspaper
The notices specify a claims period of at least two months
The PR distributes the estate having regard only to notified claims, without personal liability for claims that surface later
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That is the whole mechanism: advertise, wait out the notice period, then distribute — the protection only attaches once the period has actually run.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the notice period has to be advertised and allowed to run in full before distribution is protected; distributing early defeats the whole point of the procedure.

parts.heading: The Benjamin order: when advertising isn't enough
parts.voice: case-narrative — introduces the gap that s 27 doesn't close
body: Section 27 solves the problem of an unknown claimant who simply hasn't come forward. It does not solve a different problem: what if the PR knows a beneficiary should exist, or once existed, but cannot establish whether they are alive, dead, or where they are — a missing beneficiary rather than an unknown claim?

That gap is what Re Benjamin [1902] 1 Ch 723 addresses. The court can make an order permitting the PR to distribute the estate on a stated assumption — for example, that a missing beneficiary predeceased the testator — after the PR has made all reasonable inquiries to trace them. The order protects the PR personally from a devastavit claim if the assumption later turns out to be wrong.

A Benjamin order is not a magic wand that extinguishes the missing beneficiary's true entitlement: if that person later reappears, they can still pursue the beneficiaries who actually received the estate. What it does is exactly what s 27 does for unknown creditors — it moves the risk off the PR personally, onto the distributed assets, once the PR has done everything reasonable to find the missing person.

components.factsShort: A beneficiary under a will could not be traced despite reasonable inquiries, leaving genuine uncertainty whether he had survived the testator.
components.ratioShort: Where a beneficiary's survival or whereabouts cannot be established despite proper inquiry, the court may authorise distribution on a stated assumption, protecting the PR personally without extinguishing the missing beneficiary's underlying right to trace the assets.

interaction.prompt: A PR has advertised under s 27, but a named beneficiary in the will — the deceased's estranged brother — cannot be located despite genuine efforts to trace him, and it is unclear whether he is alive. What should the PR consider?
options: Nothing further — the s 27 advertisement already protects against this beneficiary's claim
Applying for a Benjamin order permitting distribution on a stated assumption about the brother's fate
Simply excluding the brother from distribution with no further steps, since he cannot be found
Waiting indefinitely until the brother is located before distributing anything
interaction.trapExplanation: Section 27 protects against unknown creditors and claimants who have not come forward — it does not resolve the separate problem of a known but untraceable beneficiary. That is precisely the gap a Benjamin order is designed to close.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor explains to a lay executor that if they misapply estate assets in breach of their duties, they may have to pay compensation from their own funds. What is this form of liability called?
options: Devastavit
Breach of confidence
Vicarious liability
Strict liability under statute
testPool.explanation: Devastavit is the term for a PR's personal liability, arising from a breach of duty in administering the estate, to make good the resulting loss from their own assets.

testPool.prompt: Under s 27 Trustee Act 1925, what is the minimum period a PR must allow between advertising for claims and distributing the estate?
options: One month
Two months
Three months
Six months
testPool.explanation: Section 27 requires a stated claims period of not less than two months from the date of the advertisement before the PR may safely distribute.

testPool.prompt: A Benjamin order is later shown to have proceeded on a mistaken assumption about a missing beneficiary who was in fact alive. What is the effect on that beneficiary's underlying entitlement?
options: It is automatically extinguished by the order
It survives, and the beneficiary may pursue those who received the estate
It transfers automatically to the PR personally
It can only be recovered from the court
testPool.explanation: A Benjamin order protects the PR personally; it does not destroy the true beneficiary's underlying right. That right can still be enforced against the recipients of the estate, typically by tracing.

testPool.prompt: Which change did the Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014 make to the power of appropriation?
options: It abolished the requirement to value the appropriated asset
It removed the duplicated requirement for a separate trustee consent where the PR is also the relevant trustee
It removed the requirement for an adult, capacitous beneficiary's consent entirely
It allowed appropriation to prejudice a specific legatee where necessary
testPool.trapExplanation: The reform targeted a specific duplication — a separate trustee consent where the PR and trustee were the same person. It left in place the valuation requirement, the protection against prejudicing a specific legatee, and the need for an affected adult beneficiary's own consent.

testPool.prompt: A lay executor sells estate shares at a significant undervalue through carelessness, causing a loss to the estate. A beneficiary complains. Which of the following best describes the executor's position?
options: The executor is not liable, since executors act voluntarily and in good faith
The executor may be personally liable for devastavit and required to make good the loss from their own assets
The executor's liability is limited to the value of any fee they charged for acting
The executor is only liable if they acted dishonestly, not merely carelessly
testPool.trapExplanation: Devastavit does not require dishonesty. Falling below the standard of a prudent person of business managing their own affairs is enough, and the consequence is personal liability, not a liability capped by any fee charged.

testPool.prompt: A PR advertises under s 27, and the notice period expires with no claims received. Two years later, a creditor the PR had actually corresponded with before distribution — but whose claim the PR overlooked — comes forward. What is the effect of the s 27 advertisement?
options: The PR is fully protected, since the notice period has expired
The PR is not protected as against this creditor, because the PR had actual notice of the claim before distributing
The PR is protected only if the creditor's claim is for less than £10,000
The advertisement is void because the creditor was not personally notified
testPool.trapExplanation: Section 27 protects a PR who distributes having regard only to the claims of which they then have notice. A claim the PR actually knew about before distribution falls outside that protection — the advertisement protects against unknown claims, not known ones the PR failed to act on.

testPool.prompt: Before the Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014, what was the limit on the power of advancement?
options: No advancement could be made before the beneficiary reached 18
Only half of the beneficiary's presumptive share could be advanced
Advancement could only be exercised with a court order
Advancement was limited to £10,000 regardless of the size of the trust fund
testPool.trapExplanation: The pre-2014 limit was proportionate to the beneficiary's presumptive share (one-half), not a fixed sum and not dependent on age or a court order. The 2014 Act removed that one-half ceiling.

testPool.prompt: An estate includes a valuable painting. The sole residuary beneficiary, an adult with full capacity, would rather keep the painting than have it sold and the proceeds distributed. The PR values the painting at the date of transfer and no other beneficiary is affected. What power allows the PR to transfer the painting directly?
options: The power of appropriation
The power of advancement
The power of maintenance
There is no such power — all estate assets must be converted to cash
testPool.explanation: This is a straightforward use of the power of appropriation: transferring a specific asset, valued at the date of appropriation, to satisfy a beneficiary's entitlement without a sale.

testPool.prompt: Trustees hold a fund on trust for Aisha, contingent on reaching 21. She is 19 and wants funds released early to start a business, well within her presumptive share, and the trustees consider it reasonable with no prejudice to anyone else. What is the maximum they can advance under current law?
options: Half of Aisha's presumptive share only
The whole of Aisha's presumptive share
Nothing, since her interest has not yet vested
Only enough to cover documented business expenses, capped by the court
testPool.explanation: Since the 2014 reforms removed the former one-half ceiling, trustees may advance up to the whole of a beneficiary's presumptive share, subject to their ordinary duty to act reasonably and with regard to others' interests.

testPool.prompt: A PR has made genuine, thorough efforts to trace a beneficiary named in the will but cannot establish whether she is alive. What should the PR's solicitor advise as the appropriate next step before distributing?
options: Apply for a Benjamin order permitting distribution on a stated assumption
Simply distribute, since reasonable efforts to trace are themselves sufficient protection
Advertise under s 27 Trustee Act 1925 and treat that as conclusive
Wait indefinitely, since no distribution can ever be made in these circumstances
testPool.explanation: Genuine inability to establish whether a named beneficiary is alive, despite proper inquiry, is exactly the situation a Benjamin order addresses — it authorises distribution on a stated assumption and protects the PR personally if that assumption later proves wrong.

testPool.prompt: A professional executor, acting for a fee, fails to invest estate funds prudently during a lengthy administration, causing a loss compared to a reasonable investment strategy. Which standard of care applies to them?
options: The lower standard of an ordinary prudent person of business
The higher standard of care under s 1 Trustee Act 2000, reflecting their professional capacity
No standard of care applies to investment decisions during administration
Only the standard applicable to the specific asset class, set by the beneficiaries
testPool.explanation: Where a PR acts in a professional capacity for reward, the statutory duty of care under s 1 Trustee Act 2000 sets a higher standard than that owed by an unpaid lay PR.

testPool.prompt: Section 27 Trustee Act 1925 requires notice in the London Gazette and a newspaper circulating where estate land is situated. Which of the following best explains why a court-directed notice is sometimes also required?
options: Because the London Gazette notice alone is never legally valid
Because the circumstances of the estate — such as the deceased's business connections — may make further notice necessary to reach likely claimants
Because two months is otherwise not a sufficient period
Because a court-directed notice replaces the need for a newspaper advertisement
testPool.explanation: Section 27 allows for such other notice as a court would direct, precisely because the standard Gazette and local newspaper notices may not reach every category of likely claimant on particular facts.

testPool.prompt: The Inheritance and Trustees' Powers Act 2014 modernised the appropriation power inserted into which earlier statute?
options: The Administration of Estates Act 1925
The Wills Act 1837
The Law of Property Act 1925
The Senior Courts Act 1981
testPool.explanation: The power of appropriation exercisable by personal representatives derives from the Administration of Estates Act 1925, and it was this framework that the 2014 Act modernised.

testPool.prompt: Trustees are considering advancing capital to a beneficiary with a contingent interest, but another beneficiary's interest would be adversely affected by the size of the advance requested. What must the trustees do?
options: Refuse to advance any amount at all, however small
Proceed regardless, since the whole presumptive share can always be advanced since 2014
Have regard to the interests of the beneficiary who would be prejudiced before exercising the power
Obtain the court's permission for every advancement, regardless of amount
testPool.explanation: Removing the old one-half ceiling did not remove the trustees' underlying duty to exercise the power of advancement reasonably and with regard to the interests of anyone else who might be prejudiced by it.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating a statutory protection as broader than it actually is — s 27 does not cover a claim the PR already knew about, and a Benjamin order does not extinguish a true beneficiary's underlying right. Both devices manage the PR's personal risk; neither rewrites who is actually entitled to what.
